ELISA, or enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay. It's a biochemical assay for detecting and quantifying specific proteins or antigens in a sample using antibody-antigen binding coupled to an enzyme reaction. The enzyme, like horseradish peroxidase or alkaline phosphatase, catalyzes a color-producing substrate, making protein presence and concentration visible and measurable. In the most common format, a capture antibody is bound to a well. The sample, containing the target protein, is added, allowing the protein to bind the antibody. A detection antibody linked to an enzyme then binds a different epitope on that same protein. The enzyme linked to the detection antibody catalyzes a reaction producing a colored or luminescent product. This format allows for high-throughput testing by using ninety-six-well or three-hundred-eighty-four-well plates so many samples can be tested in parallel. The intensity of the color reaction, measured by optical density or luminescence, is proportional to the target protein concentration. A standard curve calibrates the measurement. Sandwich ELISA, the format described above, suits large proteins. Competitive ELISA, where the antigen competes with enzyme-linked antigen for antibodies, works better for small molecules. ELISA is widely used for COVID-19 antibody detection, hormone assays, food allergen testing, and diagnostic serology. This technique connects to proteins as the target molecules being quantified, antibodies as the key reagents where binding specificity drives selectivity, antigens as the epitopes on the target protein recognized by the antibody pair, and immunology as the immune principle underlying antigen-antibody binding.
